<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 725, the Crow Revenue Act, would transfer approximately 4,660 acres of subsurface mineral interests located within the Crow Tribe's reservation but currently owned by the Hope Family Trust, a private entity, to the Crow Tribe (the Hope Family tracts). In exchange, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) would transfer to the Hope Family Trust approximately 940 acres of federal surface interests and 4,530 acres of federal subsurface mineral interests located outside the Crow Tribe's reservation (the Bull Mountains tracts). The legislation also requires a revenue-sharing agreement between the Hope Family Trust and the Crow Tribe for the Bull Mountain Tracts, which would be mined for coal by a private corporation, Signal Peak. Before the land swap in this bill can occur, Signal Peak must offer to relinquish the Bull Mountains lease with its currently approved mining plan of operations.
The Crow Tribe is a federally recognized Tribe in south-central Montana with the fifth-largest reservation in the United States. Due to the history of allotments and land sales, land ownership on the Crow reservation is fragmented. The Hope Family Trust owns approximately 4,660 acres of land within the boundaries of the Reservation (Hope Family tracts).\1\ This land is a split estate, with the family owning the mineral rights beneath the surface but not the associated surface rights.\2\
\1\Press Release. U.S. Senator Steve Daines. (May 29, 2024). ``Daines Leads Bill to Support Crow Tribe, Prevent Bull Mountains Mine Shutdown.'' https://www.daines.senate.gov/2024/05/29/daines-leads-bill-to-support-crow-tribe-prevent-bull-mountains-mine-shutdown/.
\2\In Montana, when surface land and subsurface rights are owned by different parties, the law generally provides for the rights of the subsurface estate to have priority over the surface estate to ensure access to mineral resources. See, e.g., Stokes v. Tutvet, 134 Mont. 250, 256-57 328 P.2d 1096 (Mont. 1958). This principle is based on the general rule that the mineral estate is the ``dominant estate'', and the surface estate is ``servient.'' Hunter v. Rosebud Cnty, 240 Mont. 194, 198, 783 P.2d 927 (Mont. 1989).
BLM currently manages federal surface and subsurface interests for the Bull Mountains tracts. Signal Peak owns and operates the Bull Mountains Mine on federal lands in central Montana. As Signal Peak exhausts coal reserves in the Bull Mountains Mine, it has sought to expand its subsurface mining operations to adjacent BLM lands in the Bull Mountains tracts, which required state and federal regulatory approvals.\3\
\3\Montana 350 v. Haaland, 50 F.4th 1254, 1266 (9th Cir. 2022).
Signal Peak's Bull Mountains Mine expansion plans to extract 175 million tons of coal, which would release 240 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions over 11 years, making it one of the most significant single-point sources for greenhouse gas emissions in the country.\4\ Federal courts struck down two Trump-era environmental assessments as inadequate in addressing climate and environmental impacts.\5\ In June 2025, BLM and the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement (OSMRE) approved the mine expansion under ``emergency permitting procedures,'' which did not allow for additional public comment.
\4\Earthjustice. (April 5, 2022). ``9th Circuit Court Strikes Down Trump-Era Underground Coal Mine Expansion.'' https://earthjustice.org/ press/2022/9th-circuit-court-strikes-down-trump-era-underground-coal-mine-expansion.
\5\Ibid.; Earthjustice. (February 13, 2013). ``Landmark Court Ruling Will Protect Water Sources, Ranchers Near Bull Mountains Underground Coal Mine.'' https://earthjustice.org/press/2023/landmark-court-ruling-will-protect-water-sources-ranchers-near-bull-mountains-underground-coal-mine.
This legislation would essentially codify the Trump administration's reckless and potentially illegal approval of the mine expansion. It would undermine federal environmental law and oversight by privatizing public land for the benefit of a criminal coal company.
Many residents and ranchers oppose the mine, alleging that the company is forcing ranchers off the land by failing to provide replacement water after the mining disrupts the water supply.\6\ In court filings, the ranching groups said they're concerned that if the MT Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) fails to maintain water rules, Signal Peak will push the last ranchers off the land. ``Under DEQ's policy, if there are no ranchers in the Bull Mountains, Signal Peak has no reclamation obligations,'' the groups said in court filings.\7\
\6\Ibid.
\7\Darrell Ehrlick, Groups challenge Montana DEQ's decision to allow more coal mining for Bull Mountain Mine, Daily Montanan (Sept. 30, 2024), https://dailymontanan.com/2024/09/30/groups-challenge-montana-deqs-decision-to-allow-more-coal-mining-for-bull-mountain-mine/.
Signal Peak was only recently released from probation by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) after convictions for environmental and safety violations.\8\ These include more than 122 accidents and more than 1,600 citations for mine safety violations.\9\ To preserve the mine's reputation, Signal Peak leadership pressured mine employees ``not to report injuries that occurred while on duty, using overt and implicit pressure, threats, and bribes.''\10\ DOJ's investigation into these violations turned up a broader culture of lawlessness at Signal Peak, leading to criminal convictions of multiple members of the leadership team for embezzlement, bank fraud, cocaine trafficking, firearm violations, tax evasion, and money laundering.\11\
\8\Tom Baratta. September 19, 2024. ``Why is Daines giving away public lands?'' Montana Independent Record. (On file with the committee.)
\9\Darrell Ehrlick. (September 30, 2024). ``Groups challenge Montana DEQ's decision to allow more coal mining for Bull Mountain Mine.'' Daily Montanan. https://dailymontanan.com/2024/09/30/groups-challenge-montana-deqs-decision-to-allow-more-coal-mining-for-bull-mountain-mine/.
\10\Hiroko Tabuchi. (January 13, 2023). ``A Faked Kidnapping and Cocaine: A Montana Mine's Descent Into Chaos,'' The New York Times. https://www.nytimes.com/2023/01/13/climate/signal-peak-mine-coal.html.
\11\Ibid.
The majority amended the legislation to address specific community concerns about outdoor recreation access by converting private land and certain surface land of the Bull Mountains Mine into public land for outdoor recreation access. Still, the bill does not address the mine's environmental impacts, reduced federal oversight, or reductions in county revenue if the swap were to take place. It also does not guarantee revenue for the Crow Tribe, as the land swap remains optional and at the discretion of Signal Peak, which is a known bad actor. The company must elect to give up its active lease and approved mine plan of operations to initiate the land swap.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.
